notes: reading: Survivor benefits other than Social Security are taxable in full: they are gross income (26 U.S.C. 61(a); 72 for a survivor annuity), the investment in the contract is an unlisted amount (0), and each exclusion (101(a) life insurance, 104(a)(1) workers' compensation, 38 U.S.C. 5301 veterans' benefits) needs a fact the board does not state. They are not earned income, and not a distribution from a qualified plan for the saver's credit or 72(t) (the plan is not stated). Tax-Calculator gets them as taxable pensions (e01500 and e01700), TAXSIM in `pensions`. policyengine-us leaves them out of gross income.

reading: Rent and farm rent are qualified business income only when the person states the unadjusted basis of qualified property (not the SSTB basis) and no other trade or business (self-employment, farm operations, partnership or S corporation income): qualified property is by definition held by a qualified trade or business (26 U.S.C. 199A(b)(6)(A)), and when the person's only stated activities that could hold it are rentals, the rentals are that business. Otherwise whether a rental is a section 162 trade or business (199A(d)(1); Treas. Reg. 1.199A-1(b)(14); the 250 hours of Rev. Proc. 2019-38) is not stated, so it is not. Estate income is not qualified business income. Tax-Calculator gets a qualified rental in e27200 (with e02000) and any other rental in e02000 only; TAXSIM gets a qualified rental in `scorp` and any other rental and estate income in `intrec`. Alternatives: no rental is qualified (the basis left without effect), or every rental is (policyengine-us's default: rental_income_would_be_qualified and farm_rent_income_would_be_qualified default to true).

reading: A stated fact says that the person works in an activity only for self-employment income (Schedule C, SSTB included) and farm operations income (Schedule F): income from the person's own work in their own business, which with no other individual's work stated is material participation (26 U.S.C. 469(h)(1); Temp. Reg. 1.469-5T(a)(2)) and makes personal services a material income-producing factor (401(c)(2)(A)(i)). Partnership and S corporation income, rent and farm rent state ownership, not work: those activities are passive (469(c)(1)-(2)), with no real estate professional status (469(c)(7)) and no active participation, so no $25,000 offset (469(i)). Estate income as stated is the nonpassive part (policyengine-us states the passive part separately). Per return, a net passive loss is disallowed and carries forward to the next year (469(a)-(b)); each loss activity keeps a ratable share of the passive income (Temp. Reg. 1.469-1T(f)(2)(i)); a disallowed loss also leaves net earnings from self-employment (1.469-1T(d)(3)). No household states a loss carried in from an earlier year. A partner's self-employment earnings are not earned income under 401(c)(2) (the partner's services are not stated). Passive income other than self-employment earnings is net investment income (1411(c)(2)(A), (c)(6)); the 2026 minimum qualified business income deduction counts only Schedule C and F income (199A(i)(2)(B)). Alternatives: no activity materially participated (Schedule C and F losses suspended too, and no 401(c)(2) earned income from them), or every owner the only participant (only rentals passive). policyengine-us applies no 469 limit.
reading: Medical expenses are the stated amounts; no Medicare Part B premium is added, since none is stated.
itemized_notes: reading: Stated other health insurance premiums are not counted again: policyengine-us documents them as part of the stated premiums without Medicare Part B (variables/household/expense/health/other_health_insurance_premiums.py), so counting both would double count. Medical expenses take the premiums without Medicare Part B.
reading: Over-the-counter health expenses are left out of medical expenses: the stated amount is not said to be prescribed medicine or insulin (26 U.S.C. 213(b)) or other medical care (213(d)(1)).
